A rendering is either the act of converting or presenting something in a particular form, or the result — the thing that gets produced from that process.

Think of it this way: you take something that exists in one state — raw data, an original text, animal fat, an architectural plan, a musical composition — and you transform it into something more finished, visible, or usable. That transformation, and what it produces, is a rendering.

This single idea of taking something and producing it in a new form is what ties all the different uses of this word together.

1. A Performance or Interpretation

When a musician, actor, or singer takes a piece of work — a symphony, a scene from a play, a song — and performs it in their own way, that performance is called a rendering. The word specifically highlights that this is one person's interpretation of a pre-existing work; someone else performing the same piece would give a different rendering.

"Her rendering of the national anthem was deeply emotional."
"The actor's rendering of Hamlet was dark and slow-paced."

You often see this used when the speaker wants to emphasize the quality or character of the interpretation, not just the fact that it was performed.

2. A Translation

When a text — a book, a poem, a religious scripture, a speech — is translated from one language into another, the translated version can be called a rendering. This word choice suggests the translator didn't just mechanically swap words; they made thoughtful decisions to faithfully convey the original meaning and spirit.

"This is a beautiful rendering of Homer's Odyssey into modern English."
"Many scholars have debated the rendering of this ancient Hebrew phrase."

Using "rendering" here implies care and craft. A rough, hasty translation would not typically be called a rendering.

3. An Architectural or Artistic Drawing

In design and architecture, a rendering is a detailed illustration — either hand-drawn or computer-generated — that shows what something (a building, a room, a product) will look like before it actually exists. It is a visual preview of something not yet built or made.

"The architect showed the city council a rendering of the new stadium."
"The car company released a rendering of their upcoming electric vehicle."

These are more than rough sketches. A rendering is usually polished and realistic enough that viewers can get a vivid sense of the final result. You often see these in news articles when a new building or product is announced before construction or manufacture begins.

4. Computer Graphics and Digital Media

This is arguably the most common modern use of the word, especially in technology, gaming, animation, and web development.

In computing, rendering is the process by which a computer takes raw digital information — code, 3D models, scene data, instructions — and converts it into the actual images you see on a screen. The images it produces are called renderings (or "renders" in informal tech language).

A few examples of where this happens:

  • Video games: Your graphics card is constantly rendering frames — turning the game's data into the pixels you see, thousands of times per second.
  • Animated films: Every frame of a Pixar or DreamWorks movie is a rendering. Powerful computers spend hours or even days processing complex scene data to produce a single second of footage.
  • Web browsers: When you load a webpage, your browser "renders" the underlying HTML and CSS code into the visual layout you see.
  • Architecture and product design: Software tools can render a 3D model into a photorealistic image — this overlaps with the architectural meaning above, but here the word specifically highlights the computer's role in producing the image.

A single image produced through this process can also be called "a rendering."

"The rendering took six hours to complete on the studio's computers."
"The latest rendering of the game's jungle level looked strikingly realistic."

5. A Coat of Plaster on a Wall (Construction)

In building and construction, rendering refers to a layer of plaster, cement, or mortar applied to the outer surface of a wall — particularly the exterior of a building. It serves multiple purposes: protecting the wall from weather, smoothing out uneven surfaces, and giving the building a clean finished appearance.

"The old farmhouse was given a fresh coat of rendering."
"Lime rendering was common in traditional European buildings."

This meaning is more common in British English than American English.

6. The Processing of Animal Fat (Cooking and Industry)

Rendering also refers to the process of slowly melting down animal fat — by applying gentle heat — to separate the pure, clean fat from the bits of tissue, water, and impurities mixed in with it. The result is a smooth, purified fat that can be used for cooking or other purposes. Lard (from pork) and tallow (from beef or mutton) are both made through rendering.

"The rendering of pork fat produces lard, which was once a staple cooking fat."
"The chef began rendering the duck fat over low heat."

7. A Formal Delivery or Announcement (Legal and Official Language)

In formal, legal, or official contexts, "the rendering of" something means its official delivery or formal declaration. You most often see this with verdicts, judgments, decisions, and professional services.

"The rendering of the verdict was postponed due to a procedural issue."
"She invoiced the client for the rendering of legal services."

Here, "rendering" carries a sense of formality and finality — something officially produced and delivered.

Even though these meanings seem very different on the surface, they all share the same underlying logic. In every case, something is being taken from one form and produced in another:

  • Raw digital data → a visual image on screen (computing)
  • A composed piece of music → a live performance (performance)
  • An original text → a translation (language)
  • Architectural plans → a detailed illustration (design)
  • Raw animal fat → pure, usable cooking fat (cooking)
  • Bare brick or stone → a smooth, plastered surface (construction)
  • A legal proceeding → a formal official decision (law)

The word always involves some process of production or transformation, and it usually carries a sense that the resulting thing is finished, presentable, or in a usable form.
Which Meanings You'll Encounter Most Often

If you read about technology, gaming, or digital media: the computing meaning is everywhere.

If you read about architecture, urban planning, or product design: the architectural drawing meaning is very common.

If you read about music, theater, or literature: the performance/translation meanings come up regularly.

If you read British news or anything about construction: the plaster coating meaning appears.

The cooking and legal meanings are more specialized but still worth knowing.

A rendering is a thing produced by converting or presenting something in a particular form — whether that's a computer turning data into an image, an architect drawing a future building, a musician performing a composition, a translator converting a text, a builder coating a wall with plaster, or a court officially delivering a verdict. The word always points to a process of transformation and the result that comes from it.
